title: Parking Lot
brief: Design the class structure for a multi-floor parking lot. Vehicles arrive, are assigned a spot, park, and later leave and pay. You are designing the object model — not the UI, not the database schema.

requirements.text: A vehicle can enter, be assigned a spot, and later exit
Three vehicle types are supported: motorcycle, car, truck
Spots come in sizes; a vehicle only fits certain sizes
Fees are charged by duration, and the hourly rate differs by vehicle type
On entry, the system finds an available spot for the vehicle
Entry is refused when no suitable spot is free

constraints: A single lot with multiple floors
Single-threaded — ignore concurrent entry for this problem

variationPoints.name: pricing strategy
variationPoints.why: Rate rules change constantly in the real world — hourly, daily cap, weekend, validation stamps

variationPoints.name: spot allocation strategy
variationPoints.why: Nearest-to-entrance, floor-fill, and reserved-first are all legitimate and swappable

variationPoints.name: vehicle type
variationPoints.why: New categories (oversized, compact, disabled-permit) arrive regularly

scenarios.title: A car arrives and parks
scenarios.description: A car pulls up to the entrance. Walk through how it ends up in a spot with a ticket.

scenarios.title: A car leaves and pays
scenarios.description: Three hours later the same car leaves. Walk through how the fee is worked out and the spot freed.

scenarios.title: A motorcycle arrives and nothing suitable is free
scenarios.description: Every motorcycle spot is taken. Walk through what happens — and how it ends.

hiddenChanges.prompt: The lot is adding electric-vehicle charging spots. A charging spot is billed per kilowatt-hour consumed, not by time parked. Revise your design so it handles this — and say what you touched and why.
goodSignal: adds a new class implementing an existing pricing abstraction
no edit to existing fee-calculation code
recognises spot capability as data, not a new subclass of Spot
badSignal: adds a boolean flag such as isElectric
adds a conditional branch inside existing fee logic
adds a subclass of the concrete pricing class rather than the interface

hiddenChanges.prompt: The lot is introducing monthly passes. A pass holder must always be given a reserved spot on the ground floor if one is free; walk-in drivers never get a reserved spot. Revise your design so it handles this — and say what you touched and why.
goodSignal: adds a new allocation strategy behind the existing allocator abstraction
the lot itself does not change
reserved is a property of a spot, not a new spot subclass
badSignal: adds an isReserved branch inside the existing allocation method
adds a passHolder flag to Vehicle and checks it in the lot

probes.prompt: Weekend rates start next month. Which method in {{class}} changes, and which other classes have to know about it?
goodSignal: names a single class or a new implementation
badSignal: adds a branch or a flag

probes.prompt: {{class}} describes more than one job. If you had to split it into two classes tonight, where is the cut — and which of the two does Ticket talk to?
goodSignal: names two responsibilities and the boundary between them
says which class Ticket depends on
badSignal: says it is fine as is
splits by data rather than by job

probes.prompt: A motorcycle arrives and every motorcycle spot is taken. Which class says no, and what exactly does the caller receive — a null, an exception, a result type?
goodSignal: names a concrete result the caller must handle

probes.prompt: Spot size and vehicle size: are they a value, an enum, or a class hierarchy in your design? What would make you change that choice?
goodSignal: justifies the choice in terms of what varies
names a condition that would change it
badSignal: subclasses per size with no behavioural difference

probes.prompt: Ticket knows the entry time. Who computes the fee — Ticket, the lot, or something else — and why there rather than the other two?
goodSignal: rejects at least one of the alternatives with a reason
badSignal: the lot does it because it has the data

commonFailureModes.name: The ParkingLotManager god class
commonFailureModes.description: One class owning allocation, pricing, ticketing, payment and exit.

commonFailureModes.name: Pricing baked into the manager
commonFailureModes.description: Fee calculation as a private method with a switch on vehicle type.

commonFailureModes.name: Spot subclassed per vehicle type
commonFailureModes.description: MotorcycleSpot, CarSpot, TruckSpot — inheritance used to vary a single value.

commonFailureModes.name: Ticket as a dumb struct
commonFailureModes.description: Ticket holds fields but the manager computes everything about it.

commonFailureModes.name: Silent failure on full lot
commonFailureModes.description: Returning null from findSpot with no modelling of the refused case.

Fees are calculated on exit, not entry

strong.tradeoffs: I put pricing behind an interface rather than a method on ParkingLot because rate rules change far more often than the lot structure does. I chose composition over subclassing Spot per vehicle type, because size is a value rather than a behaviour.

decisions.alternative: A calculateFee method on ParkingLot with a switch on vehicle type
decisions.why: Rates change monthly; the lot layout does not. The seam goes where the change is.

decisions.what: Spot size is a value, not a subclass
decisions.why: The three differ by one number and no behaviour. Subclasses would be inheritance for a lookup.
Whoever chooses the spot is the only one who knows there is none.

critiquePairs.question: Weekend pricing starts next month. Which design absorbs that without editing code that already works? Click the class that makes it possible.
critiquePairs.telling: The left design puts pricing behind an interface, so a weekend rate is a new class that implements it — nothing that already works is reopened. The right design computes the fee inside ParkingLotManager, so every new rate is an edit to a method the whole lot depends on. The interface is not there for elegance; it is there because rates are the thing that changes most.

critiquePairs.question: Both designs declare a PricingStrategy interface. In only one of them does it actually carry behaviour. Click the class that proves the seam is real.
critiquePairs.telling: An interface nothing implements is a promise, not a seam. On the right, HourlyPricing implements PricingStrategy and the lot depends on the interface, so the seam carries the actual fee logic. On the left, PricingStrategy exists in the class list, nothing implements it, nothing uses it, and the exit walkthrough calls a calculateFee that ParkingLot never declares. Pattern names in the trade-offs do not make a seam; an implementer and a caller do.

critiquePairs.question: One of these designs misses requirements; the other covers them all with one class. Which has better-shaped classes — each owning one job? Click the class in that design that owns the floor-and-spot structure.
critiquePairs.telling: Missing requirements and bad structure are different faults, and they are scored separately for exactly this reason. The right design is incomplete — no pricing, no vehicle sizes — but every class it does have owns one job, and Floor is a real concept the allocation logic will need. The left design mentions everything and puts all of it in ParkingLotManager. Fixing the right design means adding classes; fixing the left one means taking a class apart.
